# Cell theory (`cell_theory`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/biology.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Life sciences (`biology`)
- Deps: needs microscope; helped by microorganisms, synthetic_dyes
- Core idea: Plants and animals grow from cells and also contain material secreted by cells. Each cell has a boundary and usually a denser kernel (nucleus), and each cell comes only from the division of an earlier cell. Growth involves both cell enlargement and division; an animal egg is one cell; injured cells can impair a whole tissue. To show it: peel the thin skin from inside an onion scale, or scrape the inside of the cheek, lay it in a drop of water under a good microscope and stain it with a little iodine solution or dye. The box-like plant cells and their nuclei are plain to see.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying Hooke discovered living cells in 1665; he saw the empty walls of dead cork and coined the word
  - Repeating Schleiden and Schwann's own error that new cells crystallise out of formless fluid
  - Crediting Virchow alone for 'every cell from a cell'; Remak showed it first
  - Expecting animal cells to be as easy to see as plant cells; they have no walls and need staining
- History: europe: 1665 – Hooke names 'cells' in cork; 1670s Malpighi and Grew describe plant tissue; 1831 Brown names the nucleus; 1838 Schleiden (plants) and 1839 Schwann (animals) state the theory; 1852–1855 Remak and 1855–1858 Virchow: cells arise only by division; 1870s–1880s Flemming describes chromosomes in dividing cells
- Read:
  - Theodor Schwann, Mikroskopische Untersuchungen über die Uebereinstimmung in der Struktur und dem Wachsthum der Thiere und Pflanzen (1839)
  - Henry Harris, The Birth of the Cell (1999)
